name: Vitamin A for eyes

lead: Vitamin A is needed to make the light-sensitive pigment of the retina and to keep the cornea and conjunctiva healthy. Severe deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia, a leading cause of preventable childhood blindness.

It appears in eye-surface products such as vitamin A eye gels and drops and in oral supplements. Small trials have looked at dry eye, ocular surface irritation and dark adaptation in macular degeneration; none targets cosmetic appearance.

paras: Vitamin A is needed to regenerate rhodopsin in rod cells, which underlies dim-light vision, and supports the surface epithelium of the eye. Deficiency dries the conjunctiva and cornea.

Preformed retinol (not carotenoids from food) can cause toxicity, including headache, nausea, liver and bone effects with chronic excess. Intake above about 4,500 micrograms a day in pregnancy has been linked to birth defects, and the tolerable upper limit for women of reproductive age is 3,000 micrograms a day.

lead: Vitamin A is a fat-soluble vitamin required for vision and for maintaining the surface tissues of the eye. It is needed to rebuild rhodopsin, the pigment in rod cells; deficiency first shows as night blindness and, when severe, as xerophthalmia, in which the conjunctiva and cornea dry out, Bitot's spots may form and the cornea can ulcerate [1]. Vitamin A deficiency is described as the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness [1].

Topical vitamin A preparations, such as eye gels used to protect the ocular surface and combination eye drops, and oral vitamin A supplements are used in some clinical settings. In looksmaxxing and wellness circles the nutrient is sometimes raised in connection with eye health and appearance, but published trials concern deficiency, dry eye and retinal conditions rather than cosmetic brightness.
Vitamin A has a narrow safety margin as preformed retinol: chronic or very large intakes cause toxicity and, in pregnancy, are linked to birth defects [1].
infobox: High retinol intake linked to birth defects

paras: Night blindness is an early, reversible sign of low vitamin A. Severe deficiency produces dryness of the conjunctiva and cornea, keratin deposits known as Bitot's spots, and, untreated, corneal ulceration and blindness [1]. In public health programmes, large periodic doses given to young children were associated with fewer cases of night blindness, xerophthalmia and Bitot's spots in a 2017 Cochrane review, as summarised in encyclopedic sources [1].

A randomised study in 120 patients under general anaesthesia for head and neck surgery compared vitamin A eye gel plus transparent tape with erythromycin ointment plus tape for protecting the eye surface [2]. Registered trials include vitamin A palmitate for delayed dark adaptation in age-related macular degeneration (n=8) and in reticular pseudodrusen (n=9) [3][4], vitamin A with carbomer for ocular surface irritation in glaucoma patients (n=30) [5], a vitamin A, vitamin E and hyaluronate eye drop versus hyaluronate alone in diabetic retinopathy patients with dry eye (n=96) [6], oral nutrition and tear film (phase 4, n=80) [7], and a Vit-A-Vision product investigation for burning and tired eyes (n=77, recruiting) [8].

A registered study of vitamin K2 (MK-7) for dark eye circles (n=34) concerns a different vitamin [9]. The registry entries list designs and populations; results are not summarised here, and none of these studies targets cosmetic whitening or brightening of the eyes.

Toxicity arises from preformed retinol in supplements rather than carotenoids in food. A single very large dose can cause blurred vision, nausea, vomiting, dizziness and headache within hours; chronic excess affects the nervous system, liver, bones and skin, and effects generally reverse when intake stops [1]. Retinol intake above 4,500 micrograms a day in pregnancy, especially in the first trimester, has been linked to birth defects, and the tolerable upper intake for women of reproductive age is 3,000 micrograms a day [1].
